title: Security vulnerabilities of AI data centers flagged at intelligence hearing

            Security vulnerabilities of AI data centers flagged at House Intelligence hearing
Hudson Institute senior fellow David Feith urged House Intelligence Committee members at a recent hearing to consider data centers as a major cybersecurity target for adversaries including China, as policymakers survey the threat landscape -- and the implications of artificial intelligence -- 25 years after the 9/11 attacks.
“During the Cold War and even after 9/11, much of our most sensitive technology lived inside government laboratories, military facilities, classified programs, and a relatively bounded defense-industrial base,” Feith said in his...

report.summary: Expert warns House Intelligence panel that AI data centers are prime cyber targets for adversaries like China, demanding new security focus.
report.background: The warning comes amid a broader reassessment of national security threats 25 years after 9/11. Historically, David Feith of the Hudson Institute notes, America's most sensitive technology lived inside government laboratories, military facilities, classified programs, and a relatively bounded defense-industrial base. Today, however, the AI boom has pushed sensitive data, algorithms, and computing power into sprawling commercial data centers operated by private companies. This shift expands the attack surface dramatically, making data centers valuable targets for state-sponsored espionage, sabotage, and intellectual-property theft. Feith's testimony before the House Intelligence Committee emphasizes that adversaries, particularly China, are likely to view these concentrated repositories of AI talent and data as strategic nodes worth penetrating. The hearing reflects growing concern in Washington that cybersecurity policy has not kept pace with the rapid consolidation of AI infrastructure in the private sector.
key_points: The traditional model of protecting secrets inside classified government facilities is outdated. AI data centers now hold high-value data in commercial, often networked, environments that are harder to defend and more exposed to remote attack.

Adversaries like China may treat AI data centers as strategic targets. They can seek to steal proprietary training data, sabotage model integrity, or insert backdoors into AI supply chains, potentially undermining U.S. economic and military advantages.

The concentration of computing resources is itself a risk. Because large-scale AI training often relies on massive clusters at specific facilities, a single cyber incident could disrupt development or compromise the integrity of widely deployed models.

The federal government is beginning to scrutinize these vulnerabilities more formally. The House Intelligence hearing signals that Congress expects clearer cybersecurity standards and information-sharing between intelligence agencies, data center operators, and AI developers.
report.impact: For the AI industry, this warning underscores that cybersecurity cannot be an afterthought. AI developers and data center operators will face mounting pressure—and likely regulation—to harden infrastructure, audit supply chains, and adopt zero-trust principles. This could add significant cost and complexity to AI development, but it also creates a competitive advantage for organizations that prioritize security. Developers will need to integrate security into every stage of model lifecycle management, from training data collection to deployment. For regular users, the main effects will be indirect: safer, more reliable AI services, but possibly reduced access to models that are deemed too risky to host in certain locations. The broader national-security implication is that protecting AI infrastructure may become a shared public-private responsibility.
report.tools: Readers following AI data center security should monitor confidential computing technologies such as Intel SGX and AMD SEV, plus zero-trust open-source tools like Open Policy Agent (OPA), Falco, and Cilium for runtime security and policy enforcement. Also track the NIST AI Risk Management Framework and CISA's cross-sector cybersecurity guidance for evolving standards.
